prompt: Using the lesson's model (radio stays connected for a 10 s tail after each request; requests extending an existing tail only add the extra time), how many seconds is the radio connected for requests at 0, 3, 20, 25 and 60 s?

options.explanation: That counts a full 10 s tail for each of the five requests, ignoring that requests at 3 s and 25 s fall inside an existing tail.
Correct. 10 s (request at 0 s) + 3 s (the 3 s request extends the tail to 13 s) + 10 s (20 s) + 5 s (the 25 s request extends 30 s to 35 s) + 10 s (60 s) = 38 s.
The three interval unions have lengths 13, 15 and 10 seconds, totalling 38; 33 undercounts their combined duration.
That is the span from first to last request, as if the radio stayed on throughout. It returns to idle between 35 s and 60 s.

workedExample:
Each request adds whichever is smaller: a full 10 s tail, or the gap since the previous request (because it only extends a tail that is still running).

```formula
ΔT_i = min(T_tail, t_i − t_{i−1})
T_on = 10 s + 3 s + 10 s + 5 s + 10 s
T_on = 38 s
where
ΔT_i: delta-T-i, the extra connected time added by request i, in seconds (s)
min: the minimum function: the smaller of its two values
T_tail: the tail, 10 s
i: the position of a request in time-sorted order, starting at 1
t_i: the time of request i, in seconds
t_{i−1}: the time of the request before it; the first request simply pays a full tail
T_on: the total connected time, the sum of every ΔT_i
s: second
In words: the first request pays 10 s, the one 3 s later adds 3 s, the one at 20 s pays 10 s, the one 5 s later adds 5 s, and the isolated one at 60 s pays 10 s.
```

The same walk as a timeline, tracking when the current tail ends:

```
time  added  total  tail ends
 0     10     10     10
 3      3     13     13
20     10     23     30
25      5     28     35
60     10     38     70
```

Total: **38 s**. Grouping requests means they share tails: the two clusters cost 13 s and 15 s, while the isolated request at 60 s costs a full 10 s.

prompt: Use the lesson’s isolated 10-second-tail model. A background app sends a 200-byte heartbeat every 20 seconds, but its requirements permit minutes of delay and platform push for incoming notifications. Which redesign best reduces the model’s repeated activity intervals?

options.explanation: The supplied fixed-tail model assigns the same interval to each request regardless of payload. Real energy consumption also depends on transfer size and radio behaviour.

options.text: Switch the heartbeat from TCP to UDP
options.explanation: Changing the transport alone does not remove the model’s one interval per heartbeat. Real transport behaviour can affect traffic and energy.

options.text: Drop the heartbeat, batch uploads every few minutes, and use the platform push service for server-to-device messages
options.explanation: Correct for the stated delay-tolerant requirements. Less frequent batching reduces isolated fixed-tail intervals; platform push can avoid a separate polling scheme but is not energy-free.

options.text: Send the heartbeat more often so the radio never goes idle, avoiding promotion costs
options.explanation: More frequent activity merges intervals into more continuous coverage in this model. Real devices have DRX and power states not represented here.

workedExample:
In the toy model each isolated request keeps the radio active for one tail, so the share of time active is the tail divided by the period between requests:

```formula
D = T_tail / P
D_20 = 10 s / 20 s = 0.5 = 50%
D_300 = 10 s / 300 s ≈ 0.033 ≈ 3.3%
where
D: the duty cycle: the fraction of time the radio is active in the model
T_tail: the tail after each request, 10 s
P: the period between requests, in seconds (s); it must be at least the tail for this simple division to hold
D_20: the duty cycle with a heartbeat every 20 s
D_300: the duty cycle when batching every 300 s (5 minutes)
s: second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: sending every 20 s keeps the radio up half the time; sending every 5 minutes cuts that to about one thirtieth.
```

This is not a measured battery reduction. Platform-managed push may share infrastructure across apps, but still has delivery, activity and energy costs.
